results.corrected_extracted: As summarized: at about the end of the first week of abstinence from heroin, total sleep time, slow-wave, REM and stage 2 sleep were reduced and sleep latency, wake after sleep onset and REM latency increased compared with healthy sleepers (Howe et al.); during the first three weeks of abstinence, prolonged sleep latency, reduced efficiency and total sleep, more arousals and less slow-wave sleep compared with healthy sleepers (Asaad et al.); after six weeks to six months of abstinence from methadone, slow-wave and REM sleep rebounded above baseline.
results.note: Findings and places right (Howe: 'around 5–7 days of acute abstinence from chronic heroin use'; ref 17 is Asaad). Added the comparison group the review names for the Asaad finding: 'compared to healthy sleepers'.

results.corrected_extracted: As summarized: more than three-quarters of people in methadone maintenance report sleep complaints and about 50% report using both illicit drugs and legal medications to help with sleep; between 30 and 90% of patients on long-term opioid therapy show signs of central apnoea in a dose-dependent way; buprenorphine treatment in 70 patients with chronic opioid use was associated with mild to severe sleep-disordered breathing with a substantial rate of hypoxaemia.
results.note: Numbers and paragraphs right. The review says about 50% 'report use of both illicit drugs and legal medications' (not 'or'), and 'a substantial rate of associated hypoxemia', not hypoxaemia in all.
Methods para 1: 'a narrative, non-systematic review of clinical trials conducted in humans'. Databases and search terms are named, but no inclusion criteria, study counts or quality appraisal.

results.corrected_extracted: As summarized: as alcohol use becomes chronic, alcohol has less of a hypnotic (sleep-promoting) effect; clinical insomnia in about 35 to 70% of alcohol users depending on the setting and stage of use, against about 15 to 30% in the general population; sleep complaints in alcohol use disorder are one of the most refractory problems to resolve, and insomnia is the most frequent complaint after stopping drinking.
results.note: Numbers right. The review says alcohol has 'less of an hypnotic effect' (not that it loses it), gives 35–70% for 'alcohol users' (its term), and calls AUD sleep complaints, not insomnia, among the most refractory.

results.corrected_extracted: As summarized: alcohol can shorten sleep latency in healthy people; in alcohol use disorder sleep latency is prolonged during drinking and acute and post-acute withdrawal, total sleep time is reduced, slow-wave sleep deficits may take months to years to recover, REM rebounds after stopping with inconsistent findings, and sleep-stage switches are increased compared with healthy controls from the second night of abstinence to as long as one to two years.
results.note: Content right. The review says alcohol 'can decrease' sleep latency in healthy persons, and names healthy controls as the comparison for more sleep-stage switches (day 2 to 1–2 years of abstinence).

results.corrected_extracted: As summarized: self-reported insomnia during early abstinence predicted drinking or relapse in several studies; longer sleep latency in the first two weeks increased the odds of relapse in one study, longer sleep latency and lower sleep efficiency after 16 days and 19 weeks were associated with lower abstinence rates at 14 months in a second, and sleep latency at 5 days did not differ between later relapsers and abstainers in a third; slow-wave and REM measures gave mixed results.
results.note: The objective-outcomes para 1 cites two supportive sleep-latency studies [34, 69] and one null [82], not one each; added the second. Subjective-outcomes para and SWS/REM paras right.

All five alcohol Early Abs cells of Table 2 are '?' (insufficient data or conflicting results); the SL and TST subsections describe prolongation and reduction in acute withdrawal. Methods: 'narrative, non-systematic review'.

results.corrected_extracted: As summarized: cannabis may improve subjective sleep in short-term use; with chronic use, withdrawal brings sleep difficulty, strange dreams, insomnia and poor sleep quality, in 32% to 76% of people experiencing withdrawal, in inpatient and outpatient studies and placebo-controlled discontinuation studies; strange dreams typically begin within days of stopping and can persist for weeks; returning to cannabis, alcohol or other sedatives to sleep is commonly observed; the sleep-promoting effect is lessened in chronic users compared with naive users.
results.note: Numbers right (32% to 76%; dreams begin 1–3 days, last 4–14, up to 45 days). The review's comparison for the weaker sleep effect is chronic versus naïve users, not a change with use.

results.corrected_extracted: As summarized: tolerance develops to the sleep-inducing and slow-wave effects with chronic use; polysomnography in withdrawal shows increased sleep onset latency and waking, reduced total sleep time, efficiency and slow-wave sleep, and REM rebound; changes can start as soon as the first night, are more noticeable in heavy use, progress over the first weeks and persist into abstinence.
results.note: Paragraphs 3–5 right. The review says changes 'can start as soon as the first night' (example: less SWS), not that all start then; heavy use means at least 5 times a week; disturbances progress over the first 2 weeks.

Clinical-correlates para 2 and pharmacotherapy para 1 match: relapse correlated with sleep problems [43]; poor sleep in abstinence 'also contributes to relapse'; THC's sleep benefit diminishes with chronic use. Causal wording is the review's.
Methods para 1: narrative, non-systematic review; databases and search terms named, but no inclusion criteria, counts or appraisal.

Alcohol pharmacotherapy paras 1–5 match: gabapentin 'largely but not entirely' positive; ramelteon and agomelatine in case series; quetiapine double-blind placebo trial; trazodone's large placebo trial; benzodiazepines often avoided.

results.corrected_extracted: As summarized: lofexidine plus oral THC gave the greatest benefit in one study, oral THC alone none; nabilone may reverse withdrawal-related sleep disruption; valproic acid gave no benefit and even some worsening of symptoms, and lithium, nefazodone and bupropion showed no definite benefit; zolpidem, mirtazapine, gabapentin and quetiapine improved sleep parameters but none conclusively reduced relapse.
results.note: The review says valproic acid 'resulted in no benefit and even some worsening of symptoms'; the anchor lumped it with 'no definite benefit'. Rest right (cannabis pharmacotherapy paras 2–4).
Cocaine pharmacotherapy paras 1–3 match. Ref 147 (modafinil) is Morgan et al. 2010, the senior author's; ref 146 (tiagabine) is also Morgan and Malison 2008, which could be flagged too.

Methadone para (only one) and buprenorphine para 3 match: methadone and electrostimulation 'not efficient'; trazodone did not help (methadone patients with PSQI 6 or more); amitriptyline vs lorazepam, 27 patients, differed only on ease of awakening.
Para 3 and Table 2 match: collisions 6.5 (2–19) vs 1 (0–4), Z −3.526, r −0.62, all 16 more after GHB; off-road 7 more, none more after placebo, Z −2.375, p 0.018 (text 'p<0.018'); pedestrians p 0.32.

Para 3 and Table 2 match: speed deviation 4.09 vs 2.76, lane deviation 1.93 vs 1.23, Z, p, r and 13/16 right; mean speed 50 vs 52, p 0.12. Values are Table 2 medians; labelling them 'median' would help.

results.corrected_locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Figure 1 legend
results.note: Content right (all rated less able, median 4 vs 1, p<0.001; 3 h p=0.001, nearly a third at 3 or higher). The six-hour 'no longer differed' statement is in paragraph 3, not paragraph 1 or the legend.

results.corrected_extracted: At the second and third drives after GHB no simulator outcome was significantly worse than after placebo; at the third drive speed deviation was greater after placebo (p = 0.017). Within the GHB arm, collisions, off-road accidents and both deviation measures at the first drive were worse than at baseline and at both later drives.
results.note: The paper reports 'no significant differences' at 3 h and 6 h; some medians were numerically higher after GHB (collisions 2 vs 1 at 3 h), so 'significantly' added. Placebo p 0.017 and para 4 within-arm comparisons (all p<0.05) right.

Dosing paragraph: four men with nausea and vomiting could not complete the one-hour drive, were replaced, only 16 completers analysed. Discussion para 7 lists one dose, no regular users (tolerance), practice effect, no multiple-comparison correction.

results.corrected_extracted: One Dutch research programme recruited 81 participants in three equal groups (heavy GHB use with multiple GHB-induced comas; regular GHB use without comas; mild polydrug use, never GHB); the coma group performed worst on verbal memory, reported more anxiety, stress, depression and impulsivity, and showed differences in brain activity during memory and emotion tasks compared with the other two groups; the group with regular use without comas showed resting-state connectivity changes compared with the never-GHB group.
results.note: Numbers and groups right. Added the paper's comparison ('compared to the other two groups') and the same paragraph's no-coma finding (resting-state changes vs No-GHB group). 'Dutch' rests on the Amsterdam affiliations; the review does not name the country.

3.3 para 3: 'No follow-up studies ... have been performed yet', reversibility unclear. Discussion para 3: 'it cannot be excluded' that abnormalities preceded GHB use and were a risk factor for (frequent) use.

results.corrected_extracted: In 14 laboratory studies (8 to 49 participants each), GHB impaired digit-symbol, memory and psychomotor performance at moderate and higher doses, with modest or no effects at the lowest doses tested; memory impairment was less than with triazolam, pentobarbital or alcohol at the doses compared. The review classes all 14 as studies of acute effects, gives no test timings, and states it remains to be established whether the amnestic effects are reversible.
results.corrected_locator: Results, opening sentence; 3.2 Acute Effect of GHB on Cognition in Human Studies, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
results.note: Numbers right (Table 2: 14 rows, N 8–49). 'None measured thinking on the following days' is not in the review and may not hold: refs 102 (Mednick 2013) and 104 (Vienne 2012) are sleep and memory-consolidation studies.

Refs 55, 109, 110 print 'Raposo Pereira F.' and refs 106–108 'Raposo P.F.'; all six list van den Brink W. Review authors include Filipa R Pereira and Wim van den Brink. Funding 'None'; no conflicts declared.

results.corrected_extracted: 48 studies (52 publications), 1774 participants: 16 psilocybin, 16 ayahuasca, 10 LSD, 2 5-MeO-DMT, 3 several, 1 mescaline; sample sizes 6 to 315 (median 18). 14 studies (29%) had a standardized treatment, placebo control and double-blind allocation; 19 (40%) a standardized treatment but no control group and/or no double-blind allocation; 15 (31%) no standardized treatment (e.g. observational studies).
results.note: All numbers right and sum to 48. The paper's categories are 'no control group and/or no double-blind allocation' (not lacking both) and 'no standardization of treatment (e.g. observational studies)', not all observational.

results.corrected_extracted: Changes were observed most consistently (in 70 to 90% of studies investigating the domain, more than 450 participants each) for depression, stress and grief; mindfulness, acceptance and emotion regulation; personality, values and attitudes; wellbeing; and social effects. At group level no worsening of psychopathology was reported, and there was no evidence of increases in suicidality, manic or psychotic symptoms or of decreases in cognitive performance, though few studies assessed these.
results.note: Para 2 and 5 right; Table 2 confirms each domain exceeds 450 participants (484 to 975). The paper says 'no evidence of increases', not 'no increase'. Wellbeing and mindfulness data come mainly from observational studies.

Adverse effects para 1 matches every count: 25 studies (52%, 550 participants), 11 (297) none, 14 (253) with 52 headaches (1–2 days), 6 sleep, 6 tension, 3 and 3, five pairs, and the single cases named.

Limitations paras 1–2 and Methods risk-of-bias para match. '72%' is as printed, though 34/48 studies outside category A is 70.8%; 'about 70%' would be safer. Funding: article charge only (DFG, Humboldt); no conflicts.

Para 1 and Table 2 match: 13/142 (9.2%); 7/90, 2/24, 4/28 recompute to 7.8%, 8.3%, 14.3%; 11 visual, 2 emotional only; seconds 69.2%, minutes 23.1%, one hours; 53.8% once; all but two within the week.

results.corrected_extracted: Flashbacks were unpleasant for 2 (1.4% of all 142) and neutral or positive for 10; one case was not sufficiently documented. No one reported impairment of daily life. One distressing case followed an exceptionally difficult session and the participant left the study; the other was a single episode during escitalopram pretreatment after psilocybin, followed by panic attacks, after which the participant left the study.
results.note: Paper: 'One case was not sufficiently documented' (Table 2 lists it as 'Unclear'). Rest right: 2/142 = 1.4%; difficult LSD session then dropout; single episode 17 days after psilocybin during escitalopram, panic attacks, dropout.

results.corrected_extracted: One participant had about 30 brief, benign visual flashbacks over seven months, which had stopped about ten months before follow-up; at follow-up (mean 31.2 months later, 12 of 13 responding, one incompletely) she was the only one who clearly reported recurrence after the end-of-study visit.
results.note: Paper: 'the only participant who clearly reported reoccurrence'; one subject was unreachable and another gave incomplete information (Table 2: two 'Unclear'). Numbers right (12/13 = 92.3%).
HPPD paragraph matches: none met DSM-V criteria; 24.0%, 5.7%, 1.3% (recomputed 0.99^142, 0.98^142, 0.97^142). Editors' calculation checks: 1 − 0.05^(1/142) = 2.09%, about 2.1%.

results.corrected_extracted: Exclusions included current or previous psychotic or major psychiatric disorder, psychotic disorder in a first-degree relative, and more than ten prior illicit drug uses (cannabis excepted). Three of the 13 had also received escitalopram, d-amphetamine or MDMA. The authors list the sample size, varied doses and substances, likely positive attitudes, follow-up only of those with flashbacks, and exclusion of people with mental disorders as limitations.
results.note: The family-history exclusion covers psychotic disorder (and seizures, cardiac, neurological), not major psychiatric disorder. Rest right. No anchor reports that funding included Mind Medicine Inc., for which Liechti consults.

plain.fix: short: Studies in one review found shorter, lighter sleep in the first weeks after stopping heroin than in good sleepers. | how 3: Many people on methadone also sleep badly, and long-term opioid use is linked with pauses in breathing during sleep.
plain.note: The short line lacked the review's comparison group (healthy sleepers). The review calls chronic opioid use 'associated with' and 'an independent risk factor' for apnoeas, not a cause.

plain.fix: how 3: In several studies, people who said they slept badly soon after stopping were more likely to drink again than those who did not.
plain.note: The relapse link rests on self-reported insomnia in several studies (objective measures were mixed) and needs its comparison group. Other lines match the review.

plain.fix: short: Studies in one review found that many people who used cannabis regularly sleep badly after stopping, often with strange dreams. | how 2: Between about a third and three quarters of those with withdrawal symptoms had sleep problems, often with strange dreams for days or weeks.
plain.note: The review says chronic or regular use, not daily; the 32–76% is of persons experiencing withdrawal, not of everyone who stops.

plain.fix: how 1: Studies gave sleep medicines to people stopping a drug, some comparing them with a dummy pill. | how 2: For alcohol, gabapentin mostly helped, but in one big trial trazodone was linked with more drinking than a dummy pill. | how 3: For cannabis, several sleep medicines helped sleep, but none clearly helped people stay off it.
plain.note: Not all were placebo trials (case series, a retrospective study, drug-versus-drug comparisons). Trazodone was compared with placebo. Lofexidine plus THC and nabilone were reported to help relapse, so 'sleep medicines' keeps the line exact.

plain.fix: but: Only 16 people who had rarely or never used GHB, one dose, no alcohol, in a lab driving machine. | how 3: Later drives that day were not clearly worse than after the dummy drink, but this small study cannot show when driving is safe again. | how 4: Four people threw up after GHB and could not finish the first drive after it, so they were left out.
plain.note: Participants were GHB-naive or occasional users (under 3 times a year) and 2 of 16 had used it before. The four could not complete the one-hour drive, not drive at all.

plain.fix: short: GHB affects memory while it works; in one study, people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than other people who used GHB or other drugs. | how 2: The review says it is not yet known whether these short-term memory effects fully wear off. | how 3: One study found that people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs but never GHB.
plain.note: Lasting effects were also studied in regular users without comas (resting-state changes versus never-GHB controls), so 'only studied after many comas' is wrong; the review never says no study tested later days; controls used other drugs.

plain.fix: but: Most studies had no blinded placebo group, and most took place in labs or ceremonies with support, not at parties or at home. | how 2: People filled in the same questionnaires before, and again in the days or weeks after. | how 4: In studies that looked for problems, headaches were most common, and one person had a severe worsening of anxiety.
plain.note: Half the studies (24 of 48) had a control group; 34 of 48 lacked a blinded placebo design. One severe anxiety exacerbation was reported, not 'a few'. 'Up to a month' gives a timing.

plain.fix: how 4: Nobody was found to have the long-lasting vision condition doctors call HPPD.
plain.note: None met DSM-V criteria during the study, but only the 13 with flashbacks were followed up, so 'nobody developed' says slightly more than the paper. Other lines match (13/142, about 1 in 11; 2 upset).
